## Intro to Today's Lab

During today's lab, you'll apply the concepts discussed during this week's lecture. Each lab consists of a range of tasks, with corresponding questions you can answer. Please note that the questions are not required and not marked, although they do provide a helpful source of formative feedback that will help you gauge your understanding. 

In this week's lab, you'll be working with data simulated based on [this paper](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/infa.12238). In this study, researchers tested the effect of infant transport modality on their total number of vocalisations during transport. Specifically, they compared infant vocalisations when infants were being pushed in buggies or being carried in backpacks. 

### Learning Objectives
At the end of this lab, you will be able to:

1. Identify hypotheses which may be tested using $t$-tests
2. Perform a power analysis for both independent- and paired-samples $t$-tests
3. Check assumptions for both independent- and paired-samples $t$-tests
4. Use jamovi to perform both independent- and paired-samples $t$-tests
5. Interpret results from both independent- and paired-samples $t$-tests

If you complete the bonus material, you'll also be able to:

1. Present your results as you would in an APA-style report
2. Interpret $t$-test results from an empirical journal article.

## Study Overview 
Researchers want to investigate whether going on walks with babies impacts their vocalisation patterns. They have two objectives:

1. Test whether there is a difference between parent-initiated and infant-initiated speech in parents who walk with their babies.

2. Investigate whether time spent vocalising differs depending on whether the parent is carrying their infant in a backpack or pushing them in a buggy.

The researchers recruited 36 participants and split them into a backpack group and a buggy group. They then sent participants on a 15-minute walk with their infant and recorded the amount of time infants spent vocalising over the course of the walk. They also recorded the time the infant spent vocalising when the parent initiated the speech, and the time the infant spent vocalising when the infant initiated the speech.


**You can download the dataset for this study [here.](https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/ttestLabData.csv)** This dataset contains the following variables:

```{r, echo = F}
dat <- read.csv('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/ttestLabData.csv')
datInfo <- data.frame(VariableName=colnames(dat),
                      Description=c('Levels: 0 = Male, 1 = Female', 'Infant age in weeks',
                                    'Transport Modality; Levels: 0 = Buggy; 1 = Backpack',
                                    'Time infant spent vocalising (in seconds)',
                                    'Time of infant-initiated conversation',
                                    'Time of parent-initiated conversation'))
 
datInfo %>%
  kbl(col.names=c('Variable Name', 'Description')) %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = F) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = T, color=baseColor, font_size = 18, align='l') %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = T, width = '4.5cm')
```

<br>

```{r testQuiz, echo = F}
     question('Which statistical test should be used to evaluate Objective 2?',
              answer('one-sample t-test'),
              answer('independent-samples t-test', correct = T),

```

<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt"> Click here for the solution </span></summary>

<br>

<span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 14pt"> Objective 1 </span>


<b> Variables: </b>

Independent Variable: Conversation Initiator

Dependent Variable: Amount of Infant Vocalisation (in seconds)

<br>

<b>Hypotheses:</b>

Null Hypothesis: There is no difference in infant vocalisation time whether the conversation is initiated by the infant or by the parent.

Alternative Hypothesis: Infant vocalisation time changes depending on whether the parent or the infant initiates the conversation. 

<br>

<b>Hypotheses in Statistical Notation:</b>

$H_0: \mu_{infantInitiated - parentInitiated} = 0$

$H_1: \mu_{infantInitiated - parentInitiated} \neq 0$

<br>

<span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 14pt"> Objective 2 </span>

<b> Variables: </b>

Independent Variable: Transportation Modality

Dependent Variable: Amount of Infant Vocalisation (in seconds)

<br>

<b>Hypotheses:</b>

Null Hypothesis: There is no difference in infant vocalisation time between buggy users and backpack users.

Alternative Hypothesis: There is a difference in infant vocalisation time between buggy users and backpack users.

<br>

<b>Hypotheses in Statistical Notation:</b>

$H_0: Vocalisation_{buggy} = Vocalisation_{backpack}$

$H_1: Vocalisation_{buggy} \neq Vocalisation_{backpack}$



</details>
</div>

## Power Analyses

After deciding on your hypotheses but before gathering data, you should run a power analysis to determine the sample necessary to capture your effect of interest.

Recall the effect size measure for $t$-tests, $d$:

```{r, echo = F}

powerThres <- data.frame(Strength = c('Weak', 'Moderate', 'Strong'),
                         d = c('= 0.2', '~ 0.5', '≥ 0.8'))

powerThres %>%
  kbl(col.names=c('Strength', 'Absolute Magnitude of d'), align = c('l', 'c')) %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = F) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = T, color=baseColor, font_size = 18) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = T, width = '4.5cm')

```



### Your Task

<div class="nobullet">
+ [ ] $\ $ Run a power analysis to determine the sample size necessary to detect an effect size of $d$ = .35 for an independent-samples $t$-test. Assume $\alpha$ = .05, power = .8, and that you will have an equal number of participants in each group.

+ [ ] $\ $ Next, conduct a power analysis to determine the sample size necessary to detect an effect size of $d$ = .35 for a paired-samples $t$-test. As before, assume $\alpha$ = .05, power = .8.

</div>

```{r powerQuiz, echo = F}

quiz(caption = 'Check Your Results',
     question_numeric('How many total participants did you need for the independent-samples t-test?',
                      answer(130, correct = T),
                      message = 'You need 130 participants in each group, or a total of 260 participants.'),
     question_numeric('How many total participants did you need for the paired-samples t-test?',
                      answer(67, correct = T),
                      message = 'You need 67 total participants.'),
     question('What is the strength of the effect size used in the power analysis?',
              answer('Weak', correct = T),
              answer('Moderate'),
              answer('Strong'),
              message = '.35 would be considered a weak effect.'))
```

## Checking Assumptions
Assumptions should always be checked before test results are evaluated. If assumptions are violated, it could indicate that the statistical results are inaccurate. 

The assumptions of an independent-samples $t$ test are:

(1) The dependent variable must be normally distributed within each group

(2) Observations must be independent of each other

(3) The two groups must exhibit approximately equal variance (homogeneity) in the dependent variable 


The assumptions of a paired-samples $t$-test are:

(1) The difference between the paired variables must be normally distributed.

(2) Participants must be independent of each other

(3) Values must be paired in some way

### Your Tasks

<div class="nobullet">
+ [ ] $\ $ Check whether the independent-samples data meet the appropriate assumptions for an independent-samples $t$-test

+ [ ] $\ $ Check whether the paired-samples data meet the appropriate assumptions for a paired-samples $t$-test

</div>

In this example, please assume that the study design was strong and there were no issues that could cause dependency between participants or observations.

<br>

```{r cyrAssumptions, echo = FALSE}
quiz(caption = 'Check Your Results',
     question("At least one of the assumptions is violated.",
              answer("True"),
              answer("False", correct = T),
              message = "The normality plots show no major issues in normality, independence can be assumed due to proper study design, and Welch's t-test should be used, so that issues with homogeneity of variance are not a concern."))
```


<div class="container">
<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt"> Click here for a hint </span></summary>
To check normality, you can use histograms and Q-Q plots. You'll need to do this for each level of `Transport` separately. Navigate to *Analyses > Exploration > Descriptives* to do this. 

To assess independence of observations/participants, you'll need to consider the design of the study. To account for potential homogeneity of variance, you should default to using Welch's $t$-test (see [Delacre et al., 2017](https://reference-global.com/download/article/10.5334/irsp.82.pdf)).

Have a look at the [lecture slides](https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Lectures/ttests_lecture.html) if you're lost. [This article](https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13428-023-02072-x) to provide helpful guidance on why we check assumptions, and why certain assumption checking methods are more strongly recommended than others.

</details>
</div>
</br>


<div class="container">
<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt"> Click here for the solution </span></summary>

<br>

<span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 14pt"> Independent-Samples $t$-tests </span>

<span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 12pt"> Checking Normality </span>
Normality can be assessed in multiple ways. Visual assessment is recommended and should be used on this course, as the statistical tests can be overly sensitive, particularly with larger sample sizes. 

To check the histograms and Q-Q plots of the dependent variable separated by Group, click *Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Explore* and add your dependent variable, `vocalisationTime`,  to the *Variables* box. Add your independent variable, `Transport`, to the *Split by* box. Open the 'Plots' drop-down and select the following options:

```{r, echo = F, fig.align= 'center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/ttests_normalityOptions.png')
```

You should get the following output:

```{r, echo = F, fig.align= 'center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/ttests_normalityPlots.png')
```

`vocalisationTime` appears to be generally normal within each `Transport` group. There is no evidence of a significant normality violation. Inspecting the Q-Q plots, you'll note that the points go very slightly off the line in the tails, but not in a concerning way. On the whole, these results indicate that the data have not violated the assumption of normality.

<span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 12pt"> Independence </span>

Assessing independence requires an understanding of the conditions under which the data were collected. You were instructed to assume the design of the study is solid, with no issues that would cause dependency, so you may consider this assumption met.

<span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 12pt"> Homogeneity of Variance </span>

To address potential heterogeneity, Welch's $t$-test should be used by default. This test accounts for heterogeity of variance, and can be run regardless of whether the assumption is violated. Instructions for how to do this can be found in the next section.


<span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 14pt"> Paired-Samples $t$-tests </span>

<span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 12pt"> Checking Normality </span>
To check normality in differences scores, first compute a variable that reflects the difference between the paired scores by navigating to *Data > Compute*, naming the new variable, and adding the appropriate formula to the formula box:

```{r, echo = F, fig.align= 'center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/ttests_computeDifferenceScores.png')
```

Then, navigate to *Analyses > Exploration > Descriptives*. Add the new difference score variable to the *Variables* box, then go to the 'Plots' tab and select 'Histogram', 'Density' and 'QQ'. 

You'll get the following output:

```{r, echo = F, fig.align= 'center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/ttests_pairedHistogram.png')
```


```{r, echo = F, fig.align= 'center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/ttests_pairedQQ.png')
```

Look at the plots - do the difference scores appear to follow a normal distribution?


Typically, if assumptions of a statistical are violated, you can't be confident that the results obtained from that test are accurate. There will be more information about possible options when assumptions are violated provided later in the semester. For the purpose of this lab, however, you can continue with the test as planned.


</details>
</div>
</br>

## Inferential Analysis

An $t$-test produces a statistic that quantifies the degree of difference between two means. Recall that you're testing the following two hypotheses:


**Objective One:**

$$H_1: \mu_{infantInitiated-parentInitiated}\neq 0$$
**Objective Two:**

$$H_1: Vocalisation_{buggy} \neq Vocalisation_{backpack}$$


### Your Tasks

<div class="nobullet">
+ [ ] $\ $ Perform the appropriate $t$-test to address each hypothesis and interpret the results with $\alpha$ = .05.

+ [ ] $\ $ Compute the effect sizes and confidence intervals associated with your analyses

</div>

```{r cyrIndT, echo = FALSE}
quiz(caption = 'Check Your Results',
     question_numeric("What is the t-statistic associated with vocalisation time? Please round your answer to two decimal places.",
              answer(-3.79, correct = T),
              answer(3.79, correct = T),
              message = 'The t-statistic associated with this test is -3.79 (or 3.79, depending on which order you entered the levels of the independent variable.'),
question("Given an alpha = .05, the difference in vocalisation time between buggy users and backpack users is significant .",
              answer('True', correct = T),
              answer('False'),
              message = 'The p-value for this test is < .001. This means that if the null hypothesis were true, the likelihood that we would see this big of a difference in vocalisation time between buggy and backpack users is less than .1%. This provides strong evidence against the null hypothesis. Practically speaking, as our p-value is less than our alpha threshold is .05, we will reject the null hypothesis and claim that there is a significant difference in infant vocalisation between buggy and backpack users.'),
question_numeric("What is the effect size associated with the paired-samples t-test? Please round your answer to two decimal places.",
              answer(0.18, correct = T),
              message = 'The effect size associated with this test is 0.18.'))
```

<div class="container">
<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt"> Click here for a hint </span></summary>

For both objectives, you should navigate to *Analyses > t-tests*. 

</details>
</div>
</br>

<div class="container">
<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt"> Click here for the solution </span></summary>

**Objective 1**
Click *Analyses > t-tests > Paired-samples T-test*. Move your paired variables, `parentInitiated` and `infantInitiated` into the 'Paired Variables' box. Select the 'Effect size' and 'Descriptives' boxes. To get the confidence intervals, you should also select 'Mean difference' and tick 'Confidence interval'. You should see the following output:


```{r, echo = F, fig.align= 'center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/ttests_pairedOutput.png')
```

The results from the paired-samples t-test suggest that there was a significant difference in vocalisation time depending on whether the parent or child initiated the conversation, as the $p$-value of < .001 is less than the $\alpha$ threshold of .05. Specifically, the conversation was significantly longer when it was started by the parent than the infant. The confidence intervals for the variables further support this; the 95% CI associated with does not contain the null value of 0. The effect size suggests there is only a small effect. 

**Objective 2**
Click *Analyses > t-tests > Independent-samples T-test*. Move your dependent variable, `vocalisationTime`, into the Dependent Variables box and your independent variable, `Transport`, into the 'Grouping Variable' box. Uncheck 'Student's' under Test and instead select 'Welch's'. Select the 'Effect size' and 'Descriptives' boxes. To get the confidence intervals, you should also select 'Mean difference' and tick 'Confidence interval'.


```{r, echo = F, fig.align= 'center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/ttests_independentOutput.png')
```

The results from the t-test suggest that infant vocalisation was significantly different between buggy and backpack users, as the $p$-value of < .001 is less than the $\alpha$ threshold of .05. The confidence intervals for the variables further support this. The effect size suggests there is a moderate effect of transport modality on infant vocalisation in the current sample. 

</details>
</div>
</br>

## Bonus Material: Intepret & Report

Now that you've completed the analyses, write a mini report describing your findings. In this report, please:

+ Give a brief description of your sample as you would in a methods section. 

+ Present your results as you would in a results section.

<div class="container">
<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt"> Click here for a hint </span></summary>

There are many ways you could write this up, but you should at least include the following information:

+ alpha level
+ number of participants (n)
+ participant demographics (mean age, age sd, and age range of sample; gender distribution of sample)
+ results from assumptions checks
+ descriptive data for each group (M and SD)
+ the type of test used (independent or paired-samples?)
+ independent and dependent variables tested
+ $t$-statistics
+ degrees of freedom
+ p-values
+ confidence intervals
+ effect sizes

The proper style of reporting the results from a $t$-test looks like this:

$t$(##) = #.##, $p$ = .###, 95% CI = [#.##, #.##], $d$ = #.##.

Note that the numbers inside the curly brackets refer to the degrees of freedom. Please refer to the [lecture slides](https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Lectures/ttests_lecture.html) for a specific example.


</details>
</div>
</br>


## Bonus Material: Interpret a Results Section
For the answers to these questions, please refer to [Mireault et al., 2018.](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/infa.12238?saml_referrer)

```{r resultsSection, echo = FALSE}
quiz(caption = '',
     question('Which group had more participants?',
              answer('Parents who preferred strollers', correct = T),
              answer('Parents who preferred backpacks'),
              message = 'The stroller condition had two more participants (n = 16) than the backpack condition (n = 14)'),
     question('True or false: there was a significant difference between those who preferred strollers and those who preferred backpacks users in regards to the number of strangers who approached the participants.',
              answer("True", correct = T),
              answer('False'),
              message = 'Parents who prefer backpacks report significantly more engagement with strangers than those who prefer strollers. This information can be found in Table 1. The t-value associated with this comparison is -2.65, and one asterisk indicates that the p-value was ≤ .05'),
     question('True or false: parents who preferred strollers touched their infants significantly more than those who preferred backpacks.',
              answer('True'),
              answer('False', correct = T),
              message = "False - parents who preferred backpacks touched their infants more often than those who preferred strollers. This information is found in Table 1; the mean rating for parents who preferred strollers is 4.7, while the rating for those who preferred backpacks is 5.9. This difference is significant, as p ≤ .01."),
     question_numeric("Next, consider the GoPro data. What was the mean conversation duration of parents who carried their babies in strollers?",
              answer(52.37, correct = T),
              message = 'Parents who carried their babies in strollers spoke, on average, 52.37 seconds.'),
     question_numeric('What was the average number of infant-initiated conversations in backpack users?',
              answer(2.98, correct = T),
              message = 'Infants who were carried in backpacks initiated, on average, 2.98 conversations.'),
     question('What was the strength of the effect of transportation modality on the frequency of infant vocalisation?',
              answer('Weak', correct = T),
              answer('Moderate'),
              answer("Strong"),
              message = "The effect size associated with the comparison between backpack and stroller users in regards to infant vocalisation frequency was -0.41, which corresponds to a weak effect."),
     question_numeric('What was the t-statistic associated with the test of differences in visual scanning between infants in backpacks and those in strollers? Please round your answer to two decimal places.',
                      answer(-7.15, correct = T),
                      message = 'The t-statistic is -7.15'),
     question('Which of the following statements are true? Please select all that apply.',
              answer('Infants talked significantly longer when being carried in backpacks.'),
              answer('The standard deviation associated with frequency of dyadic conversation in the stroller condition was 3.41', correct = T),
              answer('The degrees of freedom for the independent-samples t-test is 40.'),
              answer('There were no significant age effects.', correct = T),
              answer('There was a moderate effect of transportation modality on visual scanning in infants.'),
              random_answer_order = T,
              message = 'The standard deviation associated with frequency of dyadic conversation in the stroller condition was 3.41. While infants spoke more often in backpacks (frequency measure), they did not speak significantly longer (duration measure). The degrees of freedom for the paired-samples t-test was 40, but for the independent-samples t-test it was 28. There were no significant age effects. The effect size associated with the impact of transportation modality on visual scanning is strong, rather than moderate.'))

```
